patterns.title: Delayed Feedback and Oscillation
patterns.domain: Systems and feedback traps; delayed observation, stock correction, response strength, action records, and oscillatory control

sources.author: James Clerk Maxwell
sources.title: On Governors
sources.read_method: Opened and read the original Proceedings scan, especially printed pages 270–272 (PDF pages 1–3), describing speed regulation, growing/decaying oscillatory disturbances and instability as governing power increases.
sources.supports: Historical foundation for feedback stability analysis and the distinction between strong correction and stable regulation.
sources.boundary: Mechanical governor analysis under stated mathematical assumptions, not the invention of every delay phenomenon or proof of this shower model. No general numerical gain threshold or modern controller performance is attributed to Maxwell.

sources.author: Donella H. Meadows
sources.title: Thinking in Systems: A Primer
sources.read_method: Opened and read the business-inventory delay example, printed pages 51–58 (PDF pages 67–74), including perception, response and delivery delays and alternative adjustment speeds.
sources.supports: Inventory-delay comparisons and the long-pipe shower illustration on printed page 54. They explain possible oscillation and differing delay locations, not inevitable instability or validation of this example’s response rule.
sources.boundary: Illustrative systems models and conceptual synthesis. Their trajectories are not measurements of every inventory system, universal prescriptions for waiting, or a basis for attributing every economic cycle to one cause.

current_example_check.read: Reopened and read the shower paragraph and surrounding inventory-delay discussion on printed pages 54–55.

sources.author: John D. Sterman
sources.title: Modeling Managerial Behavior: Misperceptions of Feedback in a Dynamic Decision Making Experiment
sources.read_method: Opened the original twenty-page PDF. Its searchable layer contains only the archive cover, so downloaded the same paper to temporary storage, rendered and OCR-read printed pages 321–323 and 334–335. Read introduction, stock-management structure, and analysis of decision rules and supply-line misperceptions.
sources.supports: Laboratory Beer Distribution Game behavior, estimated stock-adjustment rules and underweighting of the supply line; distinction between observed choices and fitted explanatory models.
sources.boundary: Evidence from a particular simulated distribution system with multiple actors and time lags. It neither measures Ada’s shower nor establishes that every participant or real manager ignores delays. No fitted coefficient or policy-effect estimate is transferred to the illustrative shower.

patterns.short_description: Recognize when corrective actions chase outdated conditions, then coordinate response strength, action records, and observation timing with the delays in the system.
use_when: Why can another turn overshoot before the first is felt?
Ada repeatedly turns a shower mixer before changed water arrives at the outlet; later overshoot prompts reversal.
goals: Recognize the familiar predicament before specialist terminology.
Explain the defining mechanism and distinguish neighboring concepts.

Physical transport/response delay, not delayed reporting. Water in transit is accumulated; temperature is a property, not a volume stock. Mixer and supply held steady. No exact trajectory, validated controller, or universal stability claim.
Separate hypothetical behavior, model results, documented cases, and practical editorial proposals.
mechanisms: Moderate correction and allow the earlier physical effect to arrive before reassessing.
Supply and equipment are held steady here. Waiting takes time; changing delays, disturbances, and safe limits need separate control.

visual.question: Why can another turn overshoot before the first is felt?
visual.alternative_text: Hypothetical qualitative illustration. Ada turns the shower mixer warmer. Earlier cool water still in the pipe arrives before the changed mixture. Repeating a large warmer turn can stack correction and later make the spray too hot. An alternative modest-adjustment procedure waits to assess the first change before repeating it; physical transit delay remains. One overshoot is shown here. Oscillation requires repeated reversals; delay alone does not establish it. Change: Coordinate adjustment size and timing with the physical response delay. Limitation: Supply and equipment are held steady here. Waiting takes time; changing delays, disturbances, and safe limits need separate control.
visual.caption: Hypothetical illustration. Earlier water continues arriving while the first change travels through the pipe. The two lower branches compare stacked correction with allowing an effect to arrive before reassessment. This is physical-response delay, not stale reporting; no exact temperature path or stable controller is claimed. One overshoot is shown here. Oscillation requires repeated reversals; delay alone does not establish it.
